prompt: Use the lesson's toy model: each request keeps the radio active for 10 s, and a request arriving while the radio is still active only extends that period. An app must send five small requests within one minute. Which schedule keeps the radio active for the **least** time?

options.text: One request every 12 s (at 0, 12, 24, 36 and 48 s)
options.explanation: Each gap is longer than the 10 s tail, so every request pays a full tail: about 50 s active.

options.text: All five within the first 4 s (at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 s)
options.explanation: Correct. Every later request lands inside the first request's tail and only extends it slightly, so the radio is active for about 14 s.

options.text: One request every 9 s (at 0, 9, 18, 27 and 36 s)
options.explanation: Each request arrives just before the previous tail ends, so the tails chain together: the radio stays active from 0 s to 46 s.

options.text: It makes no difference: five requests always cost five tails
options.explanation: Overlapping tails are shared in the model. Spacing determines how much they overlap.

workedExample:
1. A request that arrives while the radio is still active adds only the gap since the previous request; an isolated request adds a full 10 s tail.
2. Five requests 12 s apart are all isolated: five full tails, about 50 s.
3. Five requests 9 s apart each arrive 1 s before the previous tail ends, so the active period simply keeps being extended, from 0 s to 46 s.
4. Five requests within 4 s share one extended tail, from 0 s to 14 s.
5. So grouping work into one burst minimises active time. Real radios add promotion time, DRX and network-set timers, but the same direction holds.

prompt: Use the lesson’s isolated 10-second-tail model. A background app sends a 200-byte heartbeat every 20 seconds, but its requirements permit minutes of delay and platform push for incoming notifications. Which redesign best reduces the model’s repeated activity intervals?

options.explanation: The supplied fixed-tail model assigns the same interval to each request regardless of payload. Real energy consumption also depends on transfer size and radio behaviour.

options.text: Switch the heartbeat from TCP to UDP
options.explanation: Changing the transport alone does not remove the model’s one interval per heartbeat. Real transport behaviour can affect traffic and energy.

options.text: Drop the heartbeat, batch uploads every few minutes, and use the platform push service for server-to-device messages
options.explanation: Correct for the stated delay-tolerant requirements. Less frequent batching reduces isolated fixed-tail intervals; platform push can avoid a separate polling scheme but is not energy-free.

options.text: Send the heartbeat more often so the radio never goes idle, avoiding promotion costs
options.explanation: More frequent activity merges intervals into more continuous coverage in this model. Real devices have DRX and power states not represented here.

workedExample:
1. In the toy model, each isolated request keeps the radio active for one 10 s tail, whatever its size.
2. A heartbeat every 20 s keeps the radio active about half the time (10 s out of every 20 s).
3. Batching delay-tolerant uploads every 5 minutes cuts that to about 10 s in every 300 s, roughly one thirtieth.
4. Shrinking the payload or changing the transport leaves one tail per request, so it barely helps in this model; sending more often just keeps the radio on continuously.
5. Platform push handles server-to-device messages without a separate polling scheme. It is not energy-free, and this is a model result, not a measured battery saving.
